parsed.hook: Marlborough’s Wairau River block 13 supplies the fruit for Oyster Bay’s stainless-steel Chardonnay, picked at 22 °Brix to keep 12.5% alcohol and razor-sharp acidity that outruns most California juice at the same price.
parsed.wine_summary: Oyster Bay was the first brand to park screw-capped, cool-climate Chardonnay on American supermarket shelves for under $20, and it still sources from the original stony riverbed blocks planted in the late 1980s. Those soils are a free-draining mix of greywacke gravel and wind-blown loess; rain is half that of the coast, diurnal shift hits 12 °C, and the long hang-time pushes grapefruit pith and white-flesh peach without tropical blow-out. The house style blocks malolactic, ages on lees for five months, and leaves total acidity around 7 g/L—numbers that explain why the wine tastes like lemon-zest soda rather than buttered popcorn.
parsed.terroir_expression: Greywacke river stones heat fast during the day, radiating warmth back at night so sugars rise while malic acid stays high; loess seams hold just enough water to prevent hydric stress that would otherwise plump the berries and dilute flavor. The result is a wine with Marlborough’s signature snap but none of the passion-fruit excess you get down the road in Sauvignon Blanc blocks.
parsed.vinification_summary: Whole-cluster pressing, cold settle to 12 °C, and a long, slow fermentation in 100% stainless capture primary esters (isoamyl acetate gives the faint banana-candy top note); no malolactic means sharp malic acid survives, and five months on fine lees adds 2–3 g/L glycerol for tongue-coating texture without oak lactones.
food_pairing: Nashville hot chicken—high acid and low alcohol scrub cayenne oil and reset the palate
Linguine with clams and parsley-lemon gremolata—salinity mirrors the wine’s 7 g/L acidity and shellfish liquor
Corn and crab fritters—sweet kernel and delicate crustacean need a citrus-driven, unoaked white that won’t mask either flavor
Roasted pork belly bao buns—fat requires acid cut; no oak tannins clash with hoisin sweetness.
comparable_wines: Kim Crawford Unoaked Chardonnay — same region, same no-ML style, but slightly more tropical because it’s picked later
Chablis Pas si Petit — similar acid spine and steel, though Chablis gives chalk rather than river-stone minerality
Santa Rita 120 Chardonnay — same price bracket, but warmer vineyard site means rounder, less citrus profile.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-bodied unoaked Chardonnay with crisp citrus cut
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink within 18 months of vintage; screw cap keeps freshness but primary fruit fades fast. Store under 15 °C—no upside to aging.
parsed.value_assessment: $14-18 puts it head-to-head with Barefoot, Yellow Tail and Woodbridge; Oyster Bay delivers 1–1.5% lower alcohol and 2 g/L higher acidity, so it tastes drier and more refreshing for the same money.
parsed.market_position: You’ll find it by-the-glass at Cheesecake Factory and stacked in Kroger end-caps—this is entry-level Marlborough for drinkers who want a name they can pronounce and a cap they can twist.
parsed.insider_take: People expect buttery popcorn because the label says Chardonnay; what they get is lime spritz. If you like Sauvignon Kim Crawford, grab this for a dollar less and move on—if you want Meursault, keep walking.
